```text
1	# dev
2	
3	A thin glue layer over git, worktrees, forges and agent runtimes.
4	
5	It exists to stop four things collapsing into one:
6	
7	```
8	git remote      durable code state, the source of truth
9	git worktree    a disposable local checkout
10	herdr / tmux / zellij
11	                a per-host live runtime
12	dev             human intent: what am I working on, and what is next
13	```
14	
15	Everything derivable from git or the runtime is derived live. `dev` persists
16	only human intent Git cannot answer: task **state/owner/next action/context**,
17	stable asset identity, a catalog metadata summary, multiple repository quick
18	notes, and experiment lifecycle. Live Git status stays live; logical size
19	measurements are explicitly disposable cache.
20	
21	## The problem
22	
23	When a terminal multiplexer's sidebar is the only record of what you are
24	working on, nothing can ever be closed: closing a workspace loses the thread.
25	So the sidebar grows to thirty-odd entries and stops being scannable, which
26	defeats the point of having one.
27	
28	The fix is not discipline. It is giving "what am I working on" a home outside
29	the runtime, so closing a session is just closing a session.
30	
31	Bare `dev` opens an interactive dashboard when it has a terminal, and prints
32	the plain listing when piped — so `dev | grep` and `dev > file` behave as
33	expected.
34	
35	```
36	$ dev ls
37	   TASK                   STATE  REPO       BRANCH                    GIT   AGE  SESSION       NEXT
38	🔥 token refresh          HOT    atp-sipui  fix/gx-security-recovery  ↑2 ●  2h   herdr:working add the regression test
39	🌤 orderbook experiment   WARM   trading    exp/orderbook-v2          clean 6d   —             compare against the baseline
40	❄️ settings redesign      COLD   website    feat/settings             clean 3w   —             pick up after the API lands
41	```
42	
43	## Install
44	
45	### Homebrew (macOS)
46	
47	```bash
48	brew install daviddwlee84/tap/dev-cli
49	dev config init  # detects this machine's repo roots and writes a config
50	```
51	
52	The formula installs the `dev` binary plus bash, zsh and fish completions. It
53	does not write into your home directory or install the bundled agent skill.
54	Each stable release updates the tap automatically. A Homebrew-owned `dev`
55	never self-replaces: `dev upgrade` delegates to the matching `brew upgrade`
56	command, which preserves Homebrew's install records, linking, rollback, and cleanup.
57	Maintainers can retry or backfill formula publication for an existing release
58	with `gh workflow run publish-homebrew.yml -f version=vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`.
59	
60	### Scoop (Windows)
61	
62	```powershell
63	scoop bucket add dev-cli https://github.com/daviddwlee84/scoop-bucket
64	scoop install dev-cli
65	```
66	
67	The manifest for each release is also attached to the GitHub release as
68	`dev-cli.json` if you prefer `scoop install <url>`.
69	
70	### Go or source
71	
72	```bash
73	go install github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/cmd/dev@latest
74	# Pin @v0.2.4 instead when you need a reproducible install.
75	# Or from a checkout: make install  # also installs the bundled agent skill
76	```
77	
78	Every release also publishes `darwin/arm64`, `darwin/amd64`, `linux/amd64`,
79	`linux/arm64` (`.tar.gz`) and `windows/amd64`, `windows/arm64` (`.zip`) archives
80	with a `SHA256SUMS` file, so a binary can be verified without a Go toolchain.
81	
82	To find out whether the binary you have is current, and to update it:
83	
84	```bash
85	dev version           # what this build is, and whether it is a published release
86	dev version --check    # also ask GitHub for the newest release (cached for a day)
87	dev doctor            # reports the running version, install owner/path, and PATH collisions
88	dev upgrade --check    # report whether a newer release exists
89	dev upgrade            # delegate to its owner, or verify and replace a standalone binary
90	```
91	
92	`dev upgrade` replaces the binary in place only for a standalone install. If
93	Homebrew, Scoop or `go install` owns the file, it runs that tool's upgrade
94	command instead; release automation advances the Homebrew tap so that command
95	can see every stable tag. Once a day an interactive `dev` command prints a one-line hint
96	when a newer release is cached; set `[update] check = false` in `config.toml`
97	(or export `DEV_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1`) to silence it. Every network call here is
98	either explicit or a best-effort background refresh — `dev --version` and
99	`dev doctor` stay local and work offline.
100	
101	### Windows
102	
103	`dev` builds and runs on Windows, and core commands work. There is no tmux,
104	Zellij or Herdr there, so `dev` uses the no-multiplexer backend (it prints a
105	`cd` directive the shell wrapper consumes). Use the PowerShell wrapper:
106	
107	```powershell
108	Invoke-Expression (& dev shell-init powershell | Out-String)
109	```
110	
111	For a non-Homebrew install, generate completion files wherever your shell loads
112	them:
113	
114	```bash
115	mkdir -p ~/.zfunc ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions ~/.config/fish/completions
116	dev completion zsh  > ~/.zfunc/_dev
117	dev completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/dev
118	dev completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/dev.fish
119	```
120	
121	Tab completion includes commands and flags plus local tasks, repositories,
122	worktrees, help topics and bundled gitignore templates. Completion never queries
123	a forge or the network.
124	
125	Add the directory-changing wrapper to your shell rc file:
126	
127	```bash
128	eval "$(dev shell-init zsh)"      # zsh
129	eval "$(dev shell-init bash)"     # bash
130	dev shell-init fish | source      # fish
131	```
132	
133	```powershell
134	Invoke-Expression (& dev shell-init powershell | Out-String)   # PowerShell
135	```
136	
137	A child process cannot change its parent's working directory, so the wrapper
138	passes directory changes back through a private, child-only file descriptor
139	while leaving normal stdout/stderr connected to the terminal. That preserves
140	the interactive TUI and normal pipe behavior.
141	
142	The agent skill is an explicit, optional post-install step:
143	
144	```bash
145	dev skill install
146	dev skill list    # project + global skills, agents and sources
147	dev doctor       # what works on this machine, and what degrades
148	```
149	
150	Only **git** is required at runtime. `herdr`, `tmux`, `zellij`, `gh`, `glab` and
151	Azure CLI each enable more and degrade cleanly when absent.
152	
153	## Create, clone, or set up a repository
154	
155	Repository bootstrap works from any directory. Bare `dev repo new` opens an
156	interactive flow that chooses the destination under the configured
157	`project_root`, previews the setup, and confirms before writing anything:
158	
159	```bash
160	dev repo new                                  # interactive new-repository flow
161	dev repo create api --preset agent-ready      # `create` is an alias for `new`
162	dev repo new owner/api                        # clear clone reference: preserve history/origin
163	dev repo new api --template owner/starters --template-subdir go/service
164	dev repo new api --check-in stage -m "chore: initialize api"
165	dev repo clone owner/api                      # owner/name or a Git URL
166	dev repo setup . --preset agent-ready         # add the same setup to an existing repo
167	```
168	
169	`repo new NAME` keeps the small scripted default: `main`, README, and an
170	initial commit. When the argument is clearly a Git URL, local Git path, or
171	owner/name, however, `new`/`create` routes to the clone flow and preserves the
172	source history and configured remote; `repo clone` remains the explicit spelling.
173	Clone can optionally apply a preset after the checkout exists, while `repo setup` repeat-safely merges native
174	initializers and preset files into a repository you already have. Custom hooks
175	and skill setup remain responsible for their own idempotency. Use `--dry-run`
176	to inspect the available plan without mutating the target repository.
177	
178	`repo new` can also start from a content snapshot rather than an empty tree.
179	`--template` accepts a local directory/repository, Git URL, or owner/name;
180	`--template-ref` selects a branch, tag, or commit, and `--template-subdir`
181	selects a confined folder within the source. The snapshot becomes a fresh Git
182	history: source `.git` metadata is never copied, template files win scaffold
183	conflicts, regular-file modes are preserved, and traversal, symlinks, and
184	special files fail before the destination is created. A local Git working tree
185	without `--template-ref` includes existing tracked files plus untracked,
186	non-ignored files; Git-ignored files are omitted. A non-Git directory snapshots
187	its complete current tree. The same `template`, `template_ref`, and
188	`template_subdir` keys can live in a preset, which makes one starter catalog
189	repository with a preset per subfolder practical.
190	
191	Human confirmation and dry-run plans preview the selected file paths (with a
192	bounded list) and warn when the source is a live local snapshot rather than a
193	commit. URL userinfo is removed from rendered summaries and errors. Filesystem
194	walking and writes are confined relative to held `os.Root` handles, and source
195	file content is read from the handle that was validated instead of reopening a
196	mutable path.
197	
198	Bootstrap's check-in is explicit:
199	
200	| `--check-in` | Result |
201	|---|---|
202	| `commit` | stage and commit generated files, then permit commit-dependent publishing/hooks |
203	| `stage` | `git add -A` for human review, but do not commit or run `after_commit` hooks |
204	| `none` | leave generated files unstaged and uncommitted |
205	| `auto` | for `repo new`, use the preset's compatible default; clone/setup otherwise perform no automatic check-in |
206	
207	`--message` supplies the commit or staged draft message. In `stage` mode dev
208	best-effort writes the worktree-local `LAZYGIT_PENDING_COMMIT`; current lazygit
209	uses it to prefill lowercase `c`. An existing different draft is preserved with
210	a warning. This is a lazygit integration detail, not Git `commit.template`.
211	Staged setup cannot create an upstream or use the worktree-creating `start`
212	handoff; review and commit it first. The existing `repo setup --commit` remains
213	a compatibility spelling for `--check-in=commit`. If the lazygit draft cannot
214	be written, dev reports a warning but keeps the successfully staged index for
215	manual review and commit.
216	
217	The built-in `agent-ready` preset adds a starter `AGENTS.md`, a common
218	`.gitignore` section, and project-scoped Claude plans. If selected, the optional
219	`agent-history-hygiene` and `project-knowledge-harness` skills are installed and
220	dev's reviewed built-in initializers create the pre-commit/gitleaks and
221	TODO/backlog/pitfalls surfaces during bootstrap; setup does not wait for a later
222	agent to happen to trigger the skill. The history initializer also ensures
223	`.specstory/.gitignore` contains rules for SpecStory's machine-local
224	`.project.json` and generated `statistics.json`—not `.specstory/history/`, which
225	remains part of the review trail. Existing custom ignore content and file mode
226	are preserved; only missing managed rules are appended. Skills with the same
227	source and identical agent targets are sent to the installer together, while
228	each skill's declared setup still runs in its own phase. Presets may also declare
229	typed inputs, repository-contained file templates, and ordered
230	`before_commit`/`after_commit`/`after_remote` hooks.
231	
232	When `gh` or `glab` is installed and authenticated, the wizard can create a
233	GitHub or GitLab upstream using the local repository name and description,
234	choose its namespace and visibility, add `origin`, and optionally push the
235	initial/current branch. Local-only is the default and published repos
236	default private. A forge or push failure leaves the local repository and any
237	already-created upstream intact, with recovery information instead of deleting
238	work.
239	
240	TTY text fields in the repository, task-start, and finish wizards support
241	inline insertion plus Left/Right, Home/End, Delete/Backspace, and Esc/Ctrl-C
242	cancellation. Arrow keys are interpreted by the editor rather than appearing
243	as literal `^[[C`/`^[[D`; piped and buffered non-TTY input keeps its existing
244	line-oriented behavior.
245	
246	The no-argument new-repository wizard places detailed file, template, input,
247	and skill questions behind a default-no “Customize preset and template
248	options?” gate. The normal `agent-ready` path therefore uses its reviewed
249	defaults; answer yes when you want to override individual choices.
250	
251	The final handoff is explicit:
252	
253	| Handoff | Result |
254	|---|---|
255	| `stay` | print the result and leave the shell where it is |
256	| `cd` | enter the repository through the trusted `shell-init` wrapper |
257	| `open` | open the configured Herdr/tmux/Zellij runtime; fall back to `cd` when runtime is `none` |
258	| `start` | continue into the existing `dev start` task wizard with this repository fixed |
259	
260	Neither bootstrap nor a default `dev start` launches a coding agent. They
261	prepare the repository, checkout, and optional runtime surface. An explicit
262	worktree-mode `dev start --run '<shell command>'` can dispatch one command to a
263	new first-class Herdr root pane; it never chooses an agent profile or permission
264	mode on the user's behalf.
265	
266	Global custom presets live in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dev/scaffolds.toml`. A project
267	may commit `.dev-cli/config.toml` for allowlisted worktree/setup wizard defaults
268	and `.dev-cli/scaffolds.toml` for project presets, templates, hooks, and skill
269	setup. Project files cannot override host paths, runtime selection, forge
270	inventory, credentials, state, stats, update policy, or TUI policy. Legacy
271	`.dev.toml` worktree settings remain readable; the `.dev-cli` files win when
272	both are present. See [Commands and configuration](docs/reference/commands-config.md#repository-bootstrap)
273	for the schema, precedence, and executable-config trust boundary.
274	
275	## The lifecycle
276	
277	| State | Git | Runtime | Meaning |
278	|---|---|---|---|
279	| 🔥 `hot` | worktree + branch | session open | working on it now |
280	| 🌤 `warm` | worktree + branch kept | session normally closed | back within days |
281	| ❄️ `cold` | committed and pushed; worktree removed | nothing | paused, reconstructible anywhere |
282	| ✅ `done` | merged | may still be open | **MERGED**, waiting for external retirement |
283	
284	READY/MERGED/RETIRED are derived milestones, not new persisted task states.
285	An agent prepares and exits; an external coordinator integrates and retires it.
286	
287	```bash
288	dev start                                            # interactive managed-task wizard
289	dev start api --task "token refresh" --base main     # non-interactive fast path → hot
290	dev start api --task "token refresh" --base main \
291	  --run 'specstory run codex -c "codex"' --focus      # dispatch, then switch to the exact new pane
292	dev park --next "add the regression test" --wip      # → warm; self-runtime stays alive until exit
293	dev park --cold --push                               # → cold, only from outside the target runtime
294	dev resume "token refresh"                           # → hot, rebuilt if needed
295	
296	dev prepare --session claude:<uuid> --plan .claude/plans/task.md
297	dev artifact finalize --intent <id> --writer-stopped # manual post-wrapper proof
298	dev done                                             # TTY finish wizard
299	dev done --ff                                        # → done/MERGED; runtime + worktree kept
300	dev retire "token refresh" --delete-branch           # external close/wait/remove → RETIRED
301	
302	dev done --pr                                        # open review; keep task/worktree
303	dev done --merged --base-ref origin/main             # verify commit-preserving merge
304	dev sweep                                            # report drift and cleanup-pending work
305	dev sweep --merged-worktrees                         # from main: audit contained linked worktrees
306	dev sweep --merged-worktrees --apply                 # confirm each safe retirement
307	```
308	
309	On a TTY, bare `dev done` reports branch ahead/behind and classifies every
310	staged, unstaged and untracked path against the base before offering
311	commit-all, discard-all or cancel. Unique discard requires typing `DROP`;
312	scripts use `--dirty=commit --message ...` or `--dirty=discard --yes`.
313	
314	### A task does not have to mean a worktree
315	
316	Choose the lightest mode that preserves the boundary you need:
317	
318	```bash
319	# No task, no branch, no worktree: just open the canonical repo for ad-hoc work.
320	dev repo open api
321	
322	# Track a quick change directly on the branch already checked out (usually main).
323	dev start api --task "fix typo" --direct
324	
325	# Use a short-lived branch in the canonical checkout, but no linked worktree.
326	dev start api --task "small feature" --branch-only --base main
327	
328	# Default: independent branch + worktree, provisioned and runtime-opened.
329	dev start api --task "token refresh" --base main
330	```
331	
332	Direct work can be parked WARM and resumed, but cannot go COLD because the
333	canonical checkout cannot be removed. `dev done` on a clean direct task needs
334	no `--ff` or `--pr`: the work is already on its destination branch.
335	
336	Start direct for one change stream, then create a normal worktree task later
337	when real parallelism appears. A new worktree starts from committed HEAD; dirty
338	main changes are deliberately not smuggled into it, so checkpoint first when
339	the parallel task depends on them.
340	
341	### Guarded Git transactions
342	
343	`dev git` wraps only operations that need durable receipts or failure recovery;
344	it does not replace ordinary Git aliases:
345	
346	```bash
347	dev git uncommit              # soft reset; save old OID/message receipt
348	dev git recommit              # commit -C the receipt, then clear it
349	dev git pull-rebase           # exact stash OID + --index restore; never stash@{0}
350	dev git amend-all             # add -A + amend --no-edit, with normal hooks
351	dev git amend-all --exclude-agent-artifacts
352	dev git setup --print         # print optional aliases; never edit config
353	```
354	
355	Published commit rewrites require `--rewrite-published`. `amend-all` includes
356	agent artifacts by default only when a project scanner is present (or the user
357	explicitly accepts `--allow-unscanned-artifacts`).
358	
359	For automation, `dev start … --json` emits one pure creation object with absolute
360	paths and transient runtime facts. Only a newly created first-class Herdr
361	worktree with a non-empty exact `root_pane_id` is a launch target; reuse,
362	fallback, Tmux, none, or missing pane data fails closed. Worktree starts use the
363	same `repo/branch` label as `dev wt create` and pins the Git-derived parent
364	checkout with Herdr `--cwd`, preserving native nested repository/worktree
365	grouping without separate provenance metadata.
366	
367	For a human one-liner, `--run '<shell command>'` uses that same exact-pane proof
368	and sends the command to the new worktree's interactive shell. It is incompatible
369	with `--json`, `--direct`, `--branch-only`, and non-Herdr runtimes. It only
370	confirms dispatch, never waits for command completion or reports its exit code;
371	add `--focus` when the caller should switch or attach after dispatch.
372	
373	Herdr-aware writer claims—`start --direct`, `start --branch-only`, and
374	`resume`—reject another recognized agent in the same canonical Git worktree.
375	Every state, including `idle`, `done`, and `unknown`, is occupied. Pure
376	`repo open`, `wt open`, and TUI Enter reuse/focus the live owner without
377	claiming another writer. `--allow-shared-checkout` is only for explicitly
378	coordinated disjoint ownership; normal new-worktree creation remains allowed.
379	
380	Task runtime handles carry their backend name and are validated against live
381	checkout coverage before reuse or close. Destructive cleanup additionally
382	resolves every covering pane. A caller inside the target, a mixed workspace, or
383	a working/blocked/waiting agent always stops retirement; unknown status needs an
384	external `--close-unknown`. `dev done` never closes or removes anything.
385	
386	### The dashboard
387	
388	Bare `dev` (or `dev tui`) opens six lists, switched with `tab`:
389	
390	- **TASKS** — the change streams dev is tracking. What am I working on.
391	- **REPOS** — durable repositories under the scan roots, with branch, dirty
392	  state, owned size, runtime, worktrees and task tally. What do I have here.
393	- **FLEET** — repository and activity facts from configured remote machines.
394	  The TUI hides this machine by default because REPOS already shows it; `a`
395	  includes local rows. Enter opens the remote checkout through Herdr when
396	  possible, then SSH. `dev fleet list` continues to include this machine.
397	- **TRY** — dated scratch experiments, including non-Git folders, with durable
398	  tags/notes and explicit active/deprecated/archived/graduated state.
399	- **REMOTE** — repositories visible through authenticated forge CLIs, including
400	  configured Azure DevOps projects, marked when a local repo or Try exists.
401	  What can I open or clone.
402	- **SKILLS** — project and global agent skills, their target agents, source and
403	  explicitly checked update state.
404	
405	The first view is constructed before runtime auto-detection, project-root lookup,
406	cache decoding, shell-based tool checks, or the optional release refresh can
407	finish. TASKS, REPOS, and TRY then publish independently from one shared local
408	load cycle; REMOTE, FLEET, and SKILLS remain lazy. A cached REMOTE/FLEET snapshot
409	is immediately usable but is tracked separately from a current live result.
410	Every requested view has its own generation, so `r` cancels the old read, a late
411	result cannot replace a newer one, a failed refresh keeps usable rows visible,
412	and a successful empty result clears obsolete rows.
413	
414	TASKS, REPOS and TRY use the same services as their non-interactive commands.
415	Git-backed Tries appear in TRY rather than being duplicated in REPOS; REMOTE
416	still knows that local checkout exists. The repo list matters on day one: with
417	forty repositories and no tasks recorded yet, a task-only dashboard would just
418	be empty.
419	
420	Navigation is vim-style, arrows alongside:
421	
422	```
423	j k        move                 ctrl+d ctrl+u   half a page
424	g G        top / bottom         h l / tab       previous / next view
425	/          filter as you type   esc             clear, then quit
426	```
427	
428	`enter` opens a selected row only when its checkout is currently valid. Inside Herdr/tmux/Zellij it
429	switches the current client; outside it exits the dashboard and attaches to
430	the target session. A COLD worktree task requires `dev resume`; a missing or
431	unregistered worktree requires `dev sweep` first so artifacts can be salvaged
432	before the task is resumed or reaped. In TASKS, `p` parks and prompts
433	for the next action and `c` edits it. In REPOS, `enter` is pure ad-hoc open,
434	`space` expands linked worktrees inline, `m` edits repository tags/summary,
435	`s` starts an isolated worktree task, and `d` starts a tracked direct task.
436	On TASKS and REPOS, `n` quick-adds a repository thought and `N` opens its notes
437	overlay. Expanded children carry their own Git/session/task state and can be
438	opened directly. In TRY, `n` creates or clones an experiment;
439	`space` opens mark/deprecate/archive/restore/graduate actions; `a` includes
440	retained history. In SKILLS, `a` opens the upstream interactive installer, `c`
441	performs the opt-in read-only network check after the local snapshot has loaded,
442	and `u` confirms before updating
443	only the selected lock-managed skill. `r` reloads local state without checking
444	the network. `?` opens the complete context-sensitive key map. That makes
445	the branch/worktree and lifecycle costs explicit rather than silently applying
446	them to every directory.
447	
448	For a one-run startup/readiness trace, name an absolute file that does not exist:
449	
450	```bash
451	DEV_TUI_TRACE=/tmp/dev-tui-trace.json dev
452	```
453	
454	The file is created with private permissions after the alternate screen is
455	restored and before a selected runtime is activated. It contains only a bounded,
456	versioned list of relative microsecond timings, aggregate row counts, and
457	categorical view/generation/outcome fields; it never includes project names,
458	paths, commands, key values,
459	URLs, runtime handles, or raw errors, and it is not written to `stats.db` or sent
460	anywhere. `tui.initial_view_returned` means the Bubble Tea view string was built,
461	not that a terminal rasterized it. Cache acceptance, live snapshot acceptance,
462	and load completion are separate events; there is no artificial “all tabs ready”
463	event because REMOTE, FLEET, and SKILLS may never be visited.
464	
465	REPOS also has an agent-handoff copy menu. Press `y`, then `y` for contextual
466	Markdown, `p` for the checkout path, `b` for the branch, `s` for runtime/agent
467	sessions, or `w` for every linked-worktree path. Parent `yy` includes the whole
468	repo; child `yy` includes only that worktree. The same full context is
469	pipe-friendly outside the TUI:
470	
471	```bash
472	dev repo context api
473	dev repo context          # current repo, even from inside a linked worktree
474	```
475	
476	**External tools are configured, not fixed.** They run through your shell in
477	the selected row's checkout; the dashboard suspends and redraws when they exit:
478	
479	```toml
480	[[tui.tools]]
481	key  = "L"
482	name = "lazygit"
483	run  = "lazygit"
484	
485	[[tui.tools]]
486	key  = "V"
487	name = "nvim"
488	run  = "nvim ."
489	
490	[[tui.tools]]
491	key  = "B"
492	name = "vibe"
493	run  = "vibe"
494	interactive = true     # load + evaluate aliases/functions after shell rc
495	
496	[[tui.tools]]
497	key  = "P"
498	name = "plans here"
499	run  = "claude-plans-here"
500	interactive = true
501	```
502	
503	`dev config init` writes the defaults out in full rather than leaving them
504	implicit, and `dev tui tools` shows what is bound here and whether each one is
505	actually installed. The dashboard checks bindings in a bounded background load
506	after its first view; unresolved or missing programs are not offered, and
507	rendering never launches a login shell. A tool cannot take a key the dashboard
508	already uses; dev reports the clash on load.
509	
510	REMOTE loads lazily, so dashboard startup never waits on the network. Its
511	private XDG cache is decoded after the first view and contains the complete
512	paginated inventory. Fresh rows are reused without network access; stale rows
513	remain searchable while a background refresh runs. Cache payload size and
514	identity fields are validated before display, and a source fingerprint binds
515	the cache to configured GH/GL hosts and Azure targets so another endpoint is
516	never seeded automatically. GitLab inventory passes `GITLAB_HOST` (or
517	`GLAB_HOST`, default `gitlab.com`) explicitly, so the current repository cannot
518	silently select another authenticated host. A successful empty provider inventory replaces old
519	rows instead of resurrecting them later. `r` forces a
520	refresh of all configured forge providers.
521	`/` searches provider, owner/name, visibility and description; `vis:private`
522	is an exact visibility filter. Enter opens a local clone,
523	and `c` confirms before cloning an absent repo into `project_root`. The same
524	inventory is available without the full-screen UI via `dev repo remote [query]`;
525	`--cached` is its instant/offline form.
526	
527	SKILLS also loads lazily, so opening the dashboard does not start Node. Its
528	plain and JSON forms are available through `dev skill list`; run with `--check`
529	only when a remote freshness check is wanted.
530	
531	Azure DevOps Services inventory is opt-in because `az repos list` requires an
532	organization and team project. Repeat the target for every project wanted:
533	
534	```toml
535	[[forge.azure_devops]]
536	organization = "https://dev.azure.com/acme"
537	project = "Platform"
538	```
539	
540	Install Azure CLI's `azure-devops` extension and authenticate with Azure CLI.
541	`dev` does not install extensions, change Azure defaults or store credentials.
542	Azure DevOps Server/on-premises is not supported by the official extension.
543	REPOS has an explicit LIVE column (`herdr:working`, `herdr:idle`, …). Multiple
544	repo sessions collapse to `herdr:N live`; expanding the repo reveals each
545	checkout and whether its session is live or closed. External and turn-scoped
546	agent worktrees remain visible with `(external)` / `(ephemeral)` labels, so the
547	tree always reconciles with WT. `H` opens the selected repo's
548	one-year activity heatmap and `e` edits config. Returning from the editor, or
549	pressing `r`, reparses config and reloads data/tool bindings without restarting
550	the TUI; a runtime-backend change is reported as requiring restart.
551	
552	REPOS includes `LATEST`, defined as the newest dirty-file mtime, commit time, or
553	task update, plus asynchronous `SIZE`. Size is portable logical bytes:
554	
555	- `checkout_bytes` excludes only the checkout root's `.git` entry.
556	- `private_git_bytes` belongs only to this checkout and is included in
557	  `owned_bytes`, the table value.
558	- `shared_git_bytes` is shown separately and never charged to every linked
559	  worktree. `+S` means shared Git storage exists but is not reclaimable with
560	  that row.
561	
562	Measurements stream in after the first frame, use a 10-minute private XDG cache,
563	and can be forced with `r`; unreadable subtrees display a lower bound (`≥`).
564	Columns and default ordering are config:
565	
566	```toml
567	[tui.repos]
568	columns = ["repo", "branch", "git", "size", "live", "latest", "worktrees", "tasks"]
569	sort = "activity"       # activity | latest | name | git | size | tasks
570	reverse = false
571	```
572	
573	In REPOS and TRY, `O` cycles sort and `R` reverses it. Structured filters include
574	`tag:important`, `remote:none`, `size:>1GiB`, `phase:deprecated` and
575	`where:archived` where applicable. Local repo probes run with bounded
576	parallelism, and the alternate screen appears before they finish.
577	
578	See `dev help tui` for the full key map.
579	
580	### Experiments and local-data risk
581	
582	`dev try <name>` keeps its low-friction positional grammar. Lifecycle management
583	uses the separate plural group, so `dev try archive` still means "open/create a
584	Try named archive":
585	
586	```bash
587	dev tries list --json                 # active, present Tries
588	dev tries list --all --sizes          # include deprecated/archived history
589	dev tries mark redis --add important --note "compare streams"
590	dev tries deprecate redis             # intent only; files do not move
591	dev tries archive redis               # reversible move under tries_root/.dev
592	dev tries restore redis
593	dev tries graduate redis -c Infra     # same service as dev graduate
594	```
595	
596	Archive is organization, **not disk reclamation**: it moves the directory to a
597	hidden location on the same filesystem and preserves its stable catalog ID.
598	Phase 1 deliberately has no `evict`, recursive delete, or automatic remote
599	backup. Safe local removal needs repo-wide ref verification and remains a
600	follow-up rather than treating "has a remote" as proof.
601	
602	The catalog also exposes personal repository tags/notes (`dev repo mark`). To
603	find local Git state at risk before any future cleanup:
604	
605	```bash
606	dev repo list --no-remote              # no configured remotes at all
607	dev repo list --local-only             # at least one branch lacks remote upstream
608	dev repo list --multiple-remotes
609	dev repo list --multiple-upstreams     # branches track more than one remote
610	dev repo list --sizes --json           # full remotes/branches/size contract
611	```
612	
613	`no remote`, `local-only branch`, and `multiple upstreams` are distinct facts.
614	They do not claim whether commit objects are present remotely; a future reclaim
615	preflight must compare every local head/tag/note/stash against actual remote
616	refs immediately before removal.
617	
618	Going cold is safe because **the branch is the identity and the directory is a
619	cache**. `dev park --cold` refuses unless the branch is pushed, and `dev resume`
620	rebuilds the checkout from `origin/<branch>`. Once that holds, the local
621	filesystem stops being a graveyard of half-finished worktrees.
622	
623	## Rich Git state
624	
625	Every inventory surface uses the same compact, starship-like status:
626	
627	```text
628	⇕⇡3⇣2 =1 +4 !2 ?3
629	```
630	
631	- `⇡` / `⇣` / `⇕` — ahead, behind, diverged
632	- `=` — conflicted paths
633	- `+` — staged paths
634	- `!` — unstaged paths
635	- `?` — untracked paths
636	
637	`dev status` and the TUI detail pane also show the unique changed-path total
638	and type breakdown (added / modified / deleted / renamed). A path staged and
639	then modified again is one changed path, while correctly appearing in both the
640	staged and unstaged categories. JSON output exposes all counts separately.
641	
642	## Worktree ownership
643	
644	Three mechanisms create git worktrees. `dev` takes one position so nobody has
645	to improvise:
646	
647	| Kind | Owner | Where | Lifetime |
648	|---|---|---|---|
649	| Feature, fix, experiment, cross-machine handoff | **`dev`** | `~/Worktrees/<repo>/<slug>` | until external `dev retire` |
650	| Harness-owned turn-scoped subagent isolation | **Claude Code** | `.claude/worktrees/` (gitignored) | owned by that harness; no history-relocation guarantee |
651	| `herdr worktree create` | **not used** — `dev` runs `git worktree add`, then `herdr worktree open --path …` | — | — |
652	
653	**If code, history, or plans must remain reviewable—or you may return tomorrow—
654	use `dev`.**
655	
656	Claude Workflow cleanup is an explicit, stricter exception to the normal
657	harness-owned lifetime. From the canonical non-bare checkout, first review:
658	
659	```bash
660	dev sweep --ephemeral-worktrees --stale-days 14
661	dev sweep --ephemeral-worktrees --json        # schema version 1; report only
662	```
663	
664	The V1 adapter reads only bounded fixed-depth structure under
665	`~/.claude/projects`; it reports normalized IDs/states/times and never emits
666	prompts, scripts, logs, result bodies, or transcript content. A candidate needs
667	one exact provider mapping, a `completed` or `killed` workflow, matching `done`
668	agent plus journal `started` and `result`, no same-ID resumed transcript, and
669	provider inactivity older than the threshold. Killed/no-result, progress, or
670	resumed evidence remains `unknown` with no attestation bypass.
671	
672	Eligibility also requires a present registered unlocked non-prunable named
673	linked worktree with matching common-dir/branch/HEAD, no staged, unstaged,
674	conflicted, untracked, ignored, or recursive-submodule content, no Git operation,
675	no task or unsafe artifact intent, a caller outside the target, and known empty
676	runtime coverage. Missing, prunable, unregistered, and orphan paths are report
677	only. Apply is interactive and confirms each item, then reacquires every proof
678	under a common-dir cleanup lock and compares a stable fingerprint before plain
679	non-force removal:
680	
681	```bash
682	dev sweep --ephemeral-worktrees --apply
683	# Optional only when separately approved and proved safe:
684	dev sweep --ephemeral-worktrees --apply --delete-branches --base main
685	```
686	
687	A clean worktree may have commits unique to its branch because the branch is
688	retained by default. Branch deletion separately requires unchanged branch/base
689	tips, containment, zero unique commits, and `git branch -d`. This flow never
690	prunes registrations, closes runtimes, deletes Claude metadata, or rescues,
691	stashes, commits, or force-removes dirty work.
692	
693	`dev` does not delegate placement to herdr because the path policy has to hold
694	on machines without herdr. It creates the checkout with plain git and asks
695	herdr only to *open* it — which still surfaces it in the sidebar grouped under
696	its parent repo with its own branch and ahead/behind row.
697	
698	`dev` refuses to create a worktree inside a repository: a checkout nested in
699	another checkout makes every indexer, file watcher and `rg` run see a second
700	copy of the tree.
701	
702	### Provisioning
703	
704	A worktree is a clean checkout — no `node_modules`, no `.venv`, no `.env`.
705	Without provisioning, every new one starts broken. `dev` copies the gitignored
706	files you list, optionally symlinks heavy directories, and runs a setup
707	command detected from the lockfiles. Included files must remain the same
708	regular file through open; source swaps and symlinked destination parents are
709	refused, existing destinations are reported as skipped, and contents are never
710	logged:
711	
712	```toml
713	[worktree]
714	include     = [".env", ".env.local"]   # only files that are ALSO gitignored
715	link        = []                       # opt-in; sharing node_modules is risky
716	post_create = "auto"                   # uv.lock → uv sync, package-lock.json → npm ci, …
717	```
718	
719	`.claude/settings.local.json` is not a universal include. Add that exact path
720	only for an explicitly selected sticky/plain-Claude launcher and verify it
721	arrives. `claude-copilot-once` preserves an existing Copilot pin and creates/
722	removes only one it added when absent; its proxy must already run.
723	`codex-copilot-once` injects backend via CLI and may auto-start its proxy path,
724	so neither wrapper needs the copied file.
725	
726	**Copy or reinstall?** Reinstalling is always correct but can take minutes;
727	copying is fast but only sound for dependency trees carrying no absolute paths.
728	That is a per-ecosystem fact, not a preference, so dev knows it:
729	
730	```toml
731	[worktree]
732	strategy = "reinstall"      # reinstall | copy | link | skip
733	
734	[worktree.strategies]
735	node = "copy"               # node_modules copies soundly
736	```
737	
738	Asking to copy a virtualenv is refused with the reason — it bakes its own
739	absolute path into `pyvenv.cfg` and `bin/activate` — and narrowed back to
740	reinstalling rather than silently producing a broken checkout.
741	
742	`dev wt plan` shows exactly what a new worktree of a repository would get:
743	which project types were detected, which tools are missing, and every file and
744	command involved. `dev wt plan --write` seeds
745	`<repo>/.dev-cli/config.toml` from it, so
746	a project can commit its own setup and every machine provisions the same way.
747	
748	```
749	$ dev wt plan
750	PROJECT  MANAGER  FROM               DEPENDENCIES  TOOL
751	node     npm      package-lock.json  node_modules  installed
752	python   uv       uv.lock            .venv         installed
753	
754	   ACTION    WHAT          WHY
755	✓  copy      .env          gitignored, so the checkout would not have it
756	✓  copy-dir  node_modules  npm dependencies, copied instead of reinstalling
757	✓  run       uv sync       uv.lock detected
758	```
759

761	
762	```bash
763	dev repo list --sizes          # repos, remote topology and owned logical size
764	dev repo list --no-remote      # find local Git with no configured backup remote
765	dev repo context api           # agent-ready paths, Git, WT, runtime and tasks
766	dev repo new                   # interactive local/published repository bootstrap
767	dev repo setup . --preset agent-ready   # safely initialize an existing repo
768	dev repo clone owner/name -c Web   # expand forge shorthand, then clone with Git
769	dev repo clone https://dev.azure.com/acme/Platform/_git/api -c Work
770	dev repo sync --all            # fetch + prune, and report what moved
771	dev fleet list                 # Git/task/runtime state from every configured machine
772	dev fleet sync api --push      # push, then safely fast-forward clean remote checkouts
773	
774	dev try redis-streams          # dated scratch directory for an experiment
775	dev tries archive redis-streams    # reversible local archive; does not delete
776	dev graduate redis-streams -c Infra --remote   # promote it into a real project
777	
778	dev pr list                    # requests you opened or were asked to review
779	dev pr list --scope local      # with head branches, joined to your worktrees
780	dev pr list --actions          # the gh/glab commands; dev prints, never runs
781	dev prompt list                # built-in read-only context recipes
782	dev prompt agents --json       # sorted profile capabilities, no private argv/shell
783	dev prompt render pr-triage    # inspect/copy the exact prompt
784	dev prompt run session-close --agent my-agent   # bounded one-shot, no user stdin
785	dev prompt open workspace-closeout . --agent my-agent  # foreground current TTY
786	
787	dev gitignore                  # .gitignore from GitHub's templates + the rest
788	dev adopt                      # import existing worktrees/sessions as tasks
789	
790	dev stats --heatmap            # where the time actually went
791	dev summary                    # current machine-wide project snapshot
792	dev journal                    # today's commits plus current task/WIP context
793	dev help worktrees             # quick-reference pages for the workflow
794	dev help wt                    # same page, reached by command name
795	```
796	
797	### Prompt handoffs
798	
799	Escalate only as far as the situation needs: use `dev status`, `dev sweep`, or a
800	lifecycle command when deterministic facts already answer the question; use
801	`dev prompt render <recipe>` to inspect or copy context; use `run` for a bounded
802	batch answer; and use `open` only when a foreground conversation can resolve a
803	semantic question.
804	
805	The built-in recipes are `pr-triage`, `session-close`, and
806	`workspace-closeout`. They collect read-only deterministic context and instruct
807	the receiver not to mutate it. `dev` never parses an agent reply, starts a loop,
808	or treats the reply as permission for `done`, `park`, `sweep`, or `retire`.
809	There is no built-in vendor or launcher: host config defines optionally
810	described profiles with independent `[agent.run]` and `[agent.open]` commands.
811	`dev prompt agents [--json]` lists their sorted capabilities while hiding argv,
812	shell source, executable directories, prompt text, environment, and config path.
813	Global explicit/default/sole selection happens before recipe collection; the
814	selected profile must support the requested mode and never falls back to another
815	profile. `--agent` completion is mode-specific. `run` receives finite prompt
816	input and defaults to a 10-minute timeout; `open` checks for a TTY before
817	collection, reserves stdin for the conversation, has no default timeout, and
818	stays in the current terminal/pane. It does not create, focus, or reuse a
819	Herdr/tmux/Zellij surface. See [Prompt handoffs](docs/guides/prompt-handoffs.md)
820	for configuration, transport, permission, closeout-audit, and rebase-conflict
821	boundaries.
822	
823	### Repository quick notes
824	
825	Quick thoughts live beside repos in dev state, not inside each checkout:
826	
827	```bash
828	dev note add "try event subscription" --repo api --tag idea
829	dev note list api
830	dev note search "event subscription"
831	dev note edit <id-or-prefix>
832	dev note delete <id-or-prefix>
833	```
834	
835	An ID prefix must be unique and at least eight characters.
836	
837	In TASKS/REPOS, `n` quick-adds and `N` opens a browse/search/edit/delete overlay.
838	A REMOTE row supports notes only after it has a local clone; TRY keeps `n` for
839	creating experiments. Add `notes` to `[tui.repos].columns` for the count;
840	repository detail shows count/latest preview, and task detail does so when the
841	task resolves to a loaded repository row.
842	
843	Durable Markdown lives under configured
844	`paths.state_dir/notes/<catalog-id>/`, defaulting to
845	`$XDG_DATA_HOME/dev/notes/<catalog-id>/`. The catalog ID survives path moves,
846	symlink indexes and linked worktrees. `dev` does not synchronize notes or
847	catalog state; synchronize both when attachments must travel between hosts.
848	The disposable `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/dev/notes.db` is only an FTS index:
849	
850	```bash
851	dev cache clear notes                    # Markdown remains
852	dev note search "event"                 # index rebuilds automatically
853	dev note reindex                         # explicit rebuild
854	```
855	
856	`repo mark --note` remains a single catalog summary and is not overwritten.
857	`dev repo list --json` always includes `notes.count` and adds
858	`latest_id`/`latest_preview`/`latest_updated` when a latest note exists;
859	`dev note list/search/show --json` expose complete note records. Structured task
860	systems such as td/beads remain optional future adapters rather than creating
861	dot-folders automatically.
862	
863	### Machine-wide summary
864	
865	`dev summary` is the quick context dump for the whole machine. It combines
866	repositories, present Tries, worktrees, tasks, runtime sessions, recovery risk,
867	latest activity and one recent commit into Markdown suitable for a person or an
868	agent. Active work is expanded; quiet projects remain in a compact index:
869	
870	```bash
871	dev summary
872	dev summary --attention
873	dev summary --detail compact --no-runtime
874	dev summary --recent-commits 3 --sizes
875	dev summary --json | jq '.projects[] | select(.active)'
876	dev summary | opencode run "give me a quick view of this machine"
877	```
878	
879	Use `dev journal` when the question has a date range, and `dev repo context`
880	when one repository needs every checkout/task/session detail.
881	
882	### Development journal
883	
884	`dev journal` emits Markdown designed for a daily/weekly report or direct input
885	to another tool. It does not invoke an AI agent or persist the generated prose:
886	
887	```bash
888	dev journal
889	dev journal --since 7d --metrics
890	dev journal --since 3mo --granularity branch
891	dev journal --author teammate@example.com --since 30d --json
892	dev journal --since 7d | opencode run "summarize this development journal"
893	```
894	
895	The default `auto` view expands commits, keeping complete repo/branch totals
896	while limiting details to the newest 100 commits. Pass `--max-commits 0` for an
897	unabridged report. The current user's report can also include source-separated
898	session/WakaTime evidence, task intent and dirty linked worktrees whose latest
899	file mtime falls inside the requested calendar-day range.
900	
901	`dev stats` draws a contribution-style heatmap from two sources: a sampler
902	watching live agent sessions (the only way to count time spent reading and
903	debugging, including sessions in external linked worktrees), and git history (which backfills the past and survives losing the
904	database). WakaTime can be imported alongside for editor time.
905	
906	```bash
907	dev stats backfill                          # seed all repos from git history
908	dev stats backfill --repo api               # seed only one repo
909	dev stats sample --interval 5m              # from cron, every five minutes
910	dev stats import-wakatime                   # optional
911	dev stats path                              # durable SQLite location
912	dev stats clear --repo api                  # guarded selective deletion
913	```
914	
915	In the TUI, select a repo and press `H`. If it has no data, `b` backfills only
916	that repo and refreshes the panel; `r` merely rereads existing stats data.
917	
918	Stats are **data**, not cache: session samples and WakaTime imports may not be
919	reconstructible. They live at `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dev/stats.db` and clearing them
920	requires a scope plus confirmation (`--repo`, `--source`, or `--all`).
921	Regenerable data lives separately:
922	
923	```bash
924	dev cache list
925	dev cache path
926	dev cache clear remote
927	dev cache clear notes          # FTS only; Markdown remains
928	dev cache clear fleet
929	dev cache clear size
930	dev cache clear gitignore
931	dev cache clear licenses
932	dev cache clear all
933	```
934	
935	Those remove only regenerable files under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/dev/` (remote
936	inventory, note FTS, size measurements and gitignore templates) and never touch
937	`stats.db`, durable note Markdown or project data.
938	
939	## Bootstrapping an existing machine
940	
941	There is nothing to migrate for ordinary use: `dev` discovers repositories
942	below `scan_roots` and at exact `repo_paths`, and never requires a particular physical layout.
943	When you want a recursive audit or a curated navigation layer, bootstrap is the
944	explicit path:
945	
946	```bash
947	dev bootstrap ~/code /mnt/work                    # recursive report, no changes
948	dev bootstrap ~/code --json                       # machine-readable inventory
949	dev bootstrap ~/code --index ~/Projects           # plan a flat symlink catalog
950	dev bootstrap ~/code --index ~/Projects --apply   # create only the ready links
951	dev bootstrap ~/old --move ~/Projects             # plan physical moves
952	```
953	
954	The scanner classifies canonical checkouts, linked worktrees, bare repositories
955	and symlink aliases, deduplicating by Git common-directory identity rather than
956	path.
957	
958	**A symlink index is the default recommendation.** It gives a flat,
959	metadata-aware navigation root while every physical repository stays exactly
960	where it was. Put the index first in `scan_roots` and that alias becomes the UI;
961	normal discovery follows direct repo symlinks and deduplicates index + physical
962	paths.
963	
964	Physical move exists, but refuses dirty repos, linked worktrees anywhere in the
965	clone, live sessions, a current shell inside, aliases that would break,
966	occupied destinations and cross-filesystem renames. A plan with any blocked row
967	moves nothing. `--config-out` writes a fresh config for the resulting root
968	without silently rewriting the user's current one. See `dev help bootstrap`.
969	
970	## Adopting work in flight
971	
972	There is nothing to migrate. `dev` discovers repositories wherever your scan
973	roots point and **never moves, renames or deletes anything** you already have.
974	`dev config init` probes the conventional locations — `~/Documents/Program`,
975	`~/src`, `~/code`, a `GHQ_ROOT`, and so on — counts the repositories in each,
976	and writes only the ones that exist:
977	
978	```
979	$ dev config init
980	wrote ~/.config/dev/config.toml
981	
982	Detected:
983	ROOT                 REPOS  ROLE
984	~/Documents/Program  40     scan root, new projects land here
985	~/src                16     scan root
986	```
987	
988	Repositories are discovered; *tasks* are not. `dev adopt` finds the work
989	already in flight — linked worktrees from any tool, live runtime sessions, and
990	local branches ahead of the default branch — and offers to record it. It skips
991	branches already merged, and the turn-scoped worktrees an agent harness cleans
992	up itself:
993	
994	```bash
995	dev adopt            # report only
996	dev adopt --apply    # record as tasks; nothing on disk changes
997	```
998	
999	A worktree you already have somewhere else keeps working exactly as it did —
1000	`dev` records the path git reports rather than relocating it. Full detail in
1001	`dev help adopting`.
1002	
1003	## .gitignore
1004	
1005	```bash
1006	dev gitignore                 # detect the languages from the repo's files
1007	dev gitignore python node     # or say so explicitly
1008	dev gitignore --offline       # cached and bundled templates only
1009	```
1010	
1011	Language sections come from [GitHub's templates](https://github.com/github/gitignore),
1012	fetched once and cached. On top of those it adds what no language template
1013	covers: the host platform's junk files, editor state, local env files, and
1014	ephemeral coding-agent state such as linked worktrees and local settings.
1015	Review artifacts such as SpecStory histories and agent plans remain trackable
1016	unless you add your own ignore rule for them.
1017	
1018	Everything it writes goes inside a delimited block, so re-running updates that
1019	block and leaves rules you added by hand alone.
1020	
1021	## Configuration
1022	
1023	`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dev/config.toml`. Write a commented starter with
1024	`dev config init`; see the effective settings with `dev config show`; open the
1025	actual file in `$VISUAL` / `$EDITOR` with either form:
1026	
1027	```bash
1028	dev edit
1029	dev config edit
1030	DEV_EDITOR=unused dev edit --editor "code --wait"   # explicit override
1031	```
1032	
1033	If the file does not exist, `edit` generates the machine-detected starter first
1034	rather than opening an empty file. Resolution is `--editor` → `$VISUAL` →
1035	`$EDITOR` → `nvim` → `vim` → `vi`.
1036	
1037	Every path is configurable, because the right answer depends on the machine —
1038	a faster volume, a different naming convention:
1039	
1040	```toml
1041	[paths]
1042	scan_roots    = ["~/Documents/Program", "~/src/tries"]
1043	repo_paths    = ["~/.local/share/chezmoi"] # exact repos outside useful roots
1044	worktree_root = "/mnt/fast/worktrees"
1045	worktree_path = "{{worktree_root}}/{{repo|lower}}/{{branch|slug}}"
1046	state_dir     = "~/.local/share/dev"        # point at a git repo to sync it
1047	```
1048	
1049	`state_dir/tasks/*.toml` stores task intent; `state_dir/assets/*.toml` stores
1050	stable repository/Try identity, tags, one metadata summary, experiment
1051	lifecycle and per-host locations; `state_dir/notes/<catalog-id>/*.md` stores
1052	multiple repository quick notes; `state_dir/artifact-intents/v1/*.json` stores
1053	versioned post-writer handoffs and commit receipts. Git status, logical byte
1054	counts and `.specstory/statistics.json` are derived rather than durable review
1055	history. Size cache lives in `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/dev/sizes-v1.json` and is safe to
1056	delete.
1057	
1058	Template variables: `worktree_root`, `repo`, `repo_path`, `branch`, `category`,
1059	`host`, `date`. Filters: `|slug` (`feat/auth/x` → `feat-auth-x`), `|lower`,
1060	`|base`. A typo in a variable name fails at load, not as a directory literally
1061	named `{{rep}}`.
1062	
1063	A flat project layout is already first-class — it needs no migration and no
1064	special mode:
1065	
1066	```toml
1067	[paths]
1068	scan_roots   = ["~/code"]
1069	project_root = "~/code"       # repo new/clone/graduate land at ~/code/<repo>
1070	worktree_root = "/mnt/fast/wt"
1071	worktree_path = "{{worktree_root}}/{{repo|lower}}--{{branch|slug}}"
1072	```
1073	
1074	Omit `--category` and canonical repos stay flat. Categories are metadata the
1075	user may choose, never a directory structure dev imposes.
1076	
1077	## Multiple machines
1078	
1079	Do not sync worktrees or runtime state. Sync branches, and let the remote be
1080	the handoff boundary:
1081	
1082	```bash
1083	dev park --cold --push      # on the machine holding the work
1084	dev resume <task> --fetch   # on the machine picking it up
1085	```
1086	
1087	`dev` records an owner host per task and refuses to resume someone else's
1088	without `--force`. Two machines committing to one branch is the reliable way
1089	to produce a conflict here; the ownership check prevents it.
1090	
1091	Configure SSH machines separately from host-local paths:
1092	
1093	```toml
1094	# $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dev/remotes.toml
1095	schema_version = 1
1096	
1097	[defaults]
1098	connect_timeout = "15s"
1099	command_timeout = "5m"
1100	cache_ttl = "15m"
1101	max_parallel = 4
1102	dev_path = "auto"
1103	
1104	[[hosts]]
1105	name = "jingle"
1106	ssh_alias = "jingle-235"
1107	```
1108	
1109	`dev fleet list` runs each machine's own `dev`, so its XDG config and paths stay
1110	host-local. Missing `dev` installations are reported as `no-dev`; unreachable
1111	hosts can fall back to the last private XDG snapshot. Cache identity includes the
1112	complete SSH endpoint, including port. The FLEET TUI view reuses the accepted
1113	REPOS snapshot for its local host instead of scanning twice, but exposes the
1114	configured remote-host inventory by default; press `a` to include this machine.
1115	Enter opens a selected path through remote Herdr when its server is active,
1116	otherwise through `ssh -t` and a login shell. The CLI output remains the full
1117	local-plus-remote inventory.
1118	
1119	`dev fleet sync <repo> --push` publishes the clean source branch, then fetches
1120	matching clones by normalized Git remote identity. Only a clean checkout of the
1121	same branch that is strictly behind is fast-forwarded. Dirty, ahead, divergent,
1122	ambiguous and unreachable targets remain untouched and make the command fail;
1123	hosts without `dev` or without that repository are explicitly ignored.
1124	
1125	## The agent skill
1126	
1127	`dev` ships the agent skill that documents it, embedded in the binary — the
1128	same pattern `herdr --skill` uses. A skill vendored separately drifts from the
1129	tool it describes, and an agent reading a stale command list is worse than one
1130	reading none.
1131	
1132	```bash
1133	dev skill list       # merged project + global inventory
1134	dev skill list --check --json
1135	dev skill add        # interactive wizard for daviddwlee84/agent-skills/skills
1136	dev skill update project-knowledge-harness --global --yes
1137	dev skill install    # → ~/.agents/skills/dev-cli, symlinked into ~/.claude/skills
1138	dev --skill          # print it, for a dotfiles installer to sync
1139	dev skill sync       # regenerate the command reference from the command tree
1140	dev skill sync --check   # fail if it has drifted — wire into CI
1141	```
1142	
1143	`dev skill add [package]` is only a shortcut into the upstream interactive
1144	wizard. It never selects all skills or agents. Listing uses an already
1145	available/cached `skills` CLI and never downloads it; add/update are explicit
1146	actions and may access the network. Project scope resolves to the current Git
1147	checkout root, so invoking the command from a nested directory gives the same
1148	inventory.
1149	
1150	The skill defers to the companion `git-workflow` skill for commit conventions,
1151	SemVer and branch naming rather than restating them. It owns what is new: the
1152	worktree ownership rule, the task lifecycle, and how `dev` and herdr divide
1153	responsibility.
1154	
1155	## Development
1156	
1157	```bash
1158	make          # fmt, vet, test, build
1159	make test
1160	make e2e      # drives the real binary through a full lifecycle in a sandbox
1161	make skill-check
1162	```
1163	
1164	Tests build throwaway repositories under `t.TempDir()` via
1165	`internal/gitx/gittest`, and the runtime adapters share one contract suite that
1166	skips backends not installed on the machine — so the suite is meaningful in CI
1167	(where only the null backend exists) and locally (where herdr and tmux do).

# Vuln 1: Stale provider claims can authorize deletion of a different worktree: `/Users/zhouhanru/Worktrees/dev-cli/feat-pr-ci-scan/internal/ephemeral/claudeworkflow/adapter.go:823`

* **Severity:** Medium
* **Category:** `improper_authorization`
* **Confidence:** 9/10
* **Related locations:** `/Users/zhouhanru/Worktrees/dev-cli/feat-pr-ci-scan/internal/ephemeral/claudeworkflow/adapter.go:320-347`, `/Users/zhouhanru/Worktrees/dev-cli/feat-pr-ci-scan/internal/ephemeral/types.go:71-89`
* **Description:** Provider ownership is bound only to a canonical pathname. `validateWorktreePath` accepts any currently registered Git worktree at lines 823-827 before enforcing the Claude worktree namespace, while `Claim` contains no provider-observed branch, HEAD, Git common-directory, or stable worktree-registration identity. Consequently, an old terminal claim is attached to whichever worktree currently occupies that path. Report-to-apply fingerprinting validates the current Git state but cannot detect that it belongs to a different checkout than the provider run.
* **Exploit Scenario:** A legitimate workflow completes and leaves stale metadata for a worktree path. The original checkout is later removed and the path reused for a different clean, unmanaged branch—or the existing checkout is switched to another branch. Once the old metadata exceeds the inactivity threshold, the replacement satisfies the independent clean/task/artifact/runtime checks and is reported as provider-verified. An operator who trusts that classification and confirms removal causes the replacement worktree to be deleted. No concurrent race is required. Forged metadata can also target an ordinary registered worktree outside `.claude/worktrees`, because the registered-target fast path bypasses containment.
* **Recommendation:** Require a non-replayable provider-to-Git identity binding and include it in locked revalidation: at minimum the expected provider namespace, run/agent-derived path and branch, provider-observed HEAD, Git common directory, and stable worktree-registration identity. Enforce canonical `.claude/worktrees` containment before accepting a registered-target match, and reject one provider identity mapped to multiple paths. If upstream metadata cannot prove that the current registration is the one created for that run, classify it as unknown and fail closed.

# Vuln 1: Provider claim replay can authorize deletion of a replacement worktree: `/Users/zhouhanru/Worktrees/dev-cli/feat-pr-ci-scan/internal/ephemeral/claudeworkflow/adapter.go:823`

* **Severity:** Medium
* **Category:** `improper_authorization`

* **Description:** Provider ownership is bound only to a canonical pathname. `validateWorktreePath` accepts any currently registered Git target at lines 823-827 before enforcing the Claude worktree namespace. The normalized `Claim` has no provider-observed branch, HEAD, common-directory, or worktree-registration generation. Consequently, stale metadata is attached to whichever worktree currently occupies that path. Report-to-apply fingerprinting only proves that the replacement remained unchanged since the report; it cannot prove it is the checkout created for the provider run.

Forged metadata can likewise name an ordinary registered worktree outside `.claude/worktrees` because the registered-target fast path bypasses containment.
* **Recommendation:** Add an explicit provider-to-Git identity fact covering immutable checkout identity, include it in candidate fingerprints, and revalidate it under the cleanup lock. Enforce canonical provider-namespace containment before accepting registered targets and reject duplicated provider identities across paths. Because the currently supported provider metadata supplies no branch, HEAD, or registration-generation evidence, its identity fact must remain unknown; those candidates should be report-only and never apply-eligible until a source can provide non-replayable identity proof.

# Building LLM-Powered Applications with Claude

This skill helps you build LLM-powered applications with Claude. Choose the right surface based on your needs, detect the project language, then read the relevant language-specific documentation.

## Before You Start

Scan the target file (or, if no target file, the prompt and project) for non-Anthropic provider markers - `import openai`, `from openai`, `langchain_openai`, `OpenAI(`, `gpt-4`, `gpt-5`, file names like `agent-openai.py` or `*-generic.py`, or any explicit instruction to keep the code provider-neutral. If you find any, stop and tell the user that this skill produces Claude/Anthropic SDK code; ask whether they want to switch the file to Claude or want a non-Claude implementation. Do not edit a non-Anthropic file with Anthropic SDK calls. (Exception: the `prompt-audit` subcommand is non-interactive and does not stop here - it records non-Anthropic provider markers in its report's stated assumptions and never proposes switching a non-Anthropic file to the Anthropic SDK.)

## Output Requirement

When the user asks you to add, modify, or implement a Claude feature, your code must call Claude through one of:

1. **The official Anthropic SDK** for the project's language (`anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `com.anthropic.*`, etc.). This is the default whenever a supported SDK exists for the project.
2. **Raw HTTP** (`curl`, `requests`, `fetch`, `httpx`, etc.) - only when the user explicitly asks for cURL/REST/raw HTTP, the project is a shell/cURL project, or the language has no official SDK.

Never mix the two - don't reach for `requests`/`fetch` in a Python or TypeScript project just because it feels lighter. Never fall back to OpenAI-compatible shims.

**Never guess SDK usage.** Function names, class names, namespaces, method signatures, and import paths must come from explicit documentation - either the `{lang}/` files in this skill or the official SDK repositories or documentation links listed in `shared/live-sources.md`. If the binding you need is not explicitly documented in the skill files, WebFetch the relevant SDK repo from `shared/live-sources.md` before writing code. Do not infer Ruby/Java/Go/PHP/C# APIs from cURL shapes or from another language's SDK.

**If WebFetch or repository access fails** (network restricted, timeouts, clone blocked): do not keep retrying - write code from the patterns and namespace/package tables in the `{lang}/` file, run the compiler or interpreter on it, and iterate on the error output. For statically-typed SDKs (C#, Java, Go) a compile-fix loop against local errors reaches working code faster than blocked network research.

## Defaults

Unless the user requests otherwise:

For the Claude model version, please use Claude Opus 5, which you can access via the exact model string `claude-opus-5`. Please default to using adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`) for anything remotely complicated. And finally, please default to streaming for any request that may involve long input, long output, or high `max_tokens` - it prevents hitting request timeouts. Use the SDK's `.get_final_message()` / `.finalMessage()` helper to get the complete response if you don't need to handle individual stream events

## Warning: API Drift - Your Training Prior May Be Stale

Several common Claude API shapes changed in 2025-2026. If you recall a pattern from training, verify it against the `{lang}/` files in this skill before writing - the rows below are the most frequent drift points:

| Area | Stale prior | Current API |
|---|---|---|
| Extended thinking | `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` | On Claude 4.6+ models: `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`. `budget_tokens` is deprecated on Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 and **rejected with a 400** on Fable 5/5.1 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 5 / 4.8 / 4.7. Pre-4.6 models still use `budget_tokens`. |
| Web search / web fetch tool type | `web_search_20250305`, `web_fetch_20250910` | `web_search_20260209`, `web_fetch_20260209` (dynamic filtering) on Opus 5/4.8/4.7/4.6, Sonnet 5, and Sonnet 4.6. Older models keep the basic variants; on Vertex AI only basic `web_search_20250305` is available (web fetch is not on Vertex) - see the Server Tools QR below. |
| PHP parameter names | snake_case wire names as named args (`max_tokens`) | Top-level named args are camelCase (`maxTokens`). Nested array keys vary by feature (e.g. `'taskBudget'`, `'skillID'`, `'mcp_server_name'`) - copy the exact key from the documented example; do not bulk-convert. |
| Managed Agents credentials | Keep secrets host-side via custom tools (the only option before vaults shipped) | Vault `environment_variable` credentials - stored by Anthropic, substituted at egress, never visible in the sandbox (`shared/managed-agents-tools.md` -> Vaults). Host-side custom tools remain the fallback for self-hosted sandboxes. |
| Files API / Skills | `client.beta.files.*` / `client.beta.skills.*` with beta `files-api-2025-04-14` / `skills-2025-10-02` | Out of beta: `client.files.*` / `client.skills.*`, no beta header. In current SDKs `client.beta.files` / `client.beta.skills` have breaking shape changes from previous versions, matching the stable namespaces - migrate per `shared/live-sources.md` -> Files API / Skills Guide. |

The `{lang}/` files in this skill are authoritative over recalled patterns.

## Language Detection

Before reading code examples, determine which language the user is working in (exception: for the `prompt-audit` subcommand, skip this section's ask steps - the audit is non-interactive and its inventory is language-agnostic; when no language is inferable, proceed without asking and state the assumption in the report):

 - `*.kt`, `*.kts`, `build.gradle.kts` -> **Java** - Kotlin uses the Java SDK, read from `java/`

### Language-Specific Feature Support

Every SDK language above supports both the beta Tool Runner and Managed Agents (beta) - Python (`@beta_tool` decorator), TypeScript (`betaZodTool` + Zod), Java (annotated classes), Go (`BetaToolRunner` in the `toolrunner` pkg), Ruby (`BaseTool` + `tool_runner`), C# (`BetaToolRunner` + raw JSON schema), PHP (`BetaRunnableTool` + `toolRunner()`); code entry points are in the Tool Use Patterns quick reference below. cURL is raw HTTP (no SDK features) and supports Managed Agents.

> **Managed Agents code examples**: see the reading guide in the `## Managed Agents (Beta)` section below.

## Which Surface Should I Use?

> **Start simple.** Default to the simplest tier that meets your needs. Single API calls and workflows handle most use cases - only reach for agents when the task genuinely requires open-ended, model-driven exploration. "Simplest" means the least code you own: for a hosted, scheduled, or memory-backed agent, Managed Agents is usually the simplest option (no loop code, no state files, no scheduler), even though it's a bigger platform.

| Use Case                                        | Tier            | Recommended Surface       | Why                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Classification, summarization, extraction, Q&A  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | One request, one response                                    |
| Batch processing or embeddings                  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | Specialized endpoints                                        |
| Multi-step pipelines with code-controlled logic | Workflow        | **Claude API + tool use** | You orchestrate the loop                                     |
| Custom agent with your own tools                | Agent           | **Claude API + tool use** | Maximum flexibility                                          |
| Server-managed stateful agent with workspace    | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Anthropic runs the loop and hosts the tool-execution sandbox |
| Persisted, versioned agent configs              | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Agents are stored objects; sessions pin to a version         |
| Long-running multi-turn agent with file mounts  | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Per-session containers, SSE event stream, Skills + MCP       |
| Agent that runs on a schedule (cron, "every night") | Agent       | **Managed Agents** - scheduled deployments | Deployments fire sessions autonomously; no client-side scheduler |

> **Note:** Managed Agents is the right choice when you want Anthropic to run the agent loop *and* host the container where tools execute - file ops, bash, code execution all run in the per-session workspace. If you want to host the compute yourself or run your own custom tool runtime, Claude API + tool use is the right choice - use the tool runner for the agentic loop - its per-turn hooks still give you approval gates, logging, error interception, and conditional execution (see `shared/tool-use-concepts.md`) - or the manual loop when you want to own the entire loop yourself.

> **Cloud-provider access.** **Claude Platform on AWS** is Anthropic-operated with same-day API parity - see `shared/claude-platform-on-aws.md` for client setup. For per-feature availability on **Claude Platform on AWS**, **Amazon Bedrock**, **Google Vertex AI**, and **Microsoft Foundry**, see `shared/platform-availability.md` - that table is the single source of truth in this skill; do not infer availability from anywhere else.

### Building an Agent: Four Approaches

Once you've decided you actually need an agent (open-ended, model-driven tool use), there are four distinct ways to build one. Two independent questions separate them: **who supplies the harness** (the agent loop + context management) and **who supplies the deployment** (the infra the agent runs on). The Tool Runner and the Claude Agent SDK both supply a *harness only* - you still host and deploy them yourself - which is why they're easy to conflate. Managed Agents (CMA) is the only option that supplies **both** the harness *and* managed deployment; the manual loop supplies neither.

| # | Approach | You write | Harness & deployment | Tools available | Use when |
|---|----------|-----------|----------------------|-----------------|----------|
| 1 | **Claude API - manual loop** | The `while stop_reason == "tool_use"` loop yourself | You build the harness; you host | Only tools you define | You want to own the *entire* loop - no beta dependency, or a control flow the Tool Runner's per-turn hooks don't fit |
| 2 | **Claude API - Tool Runner** (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner` + `@beta_tool` / `betaZodTool`) | Just the tool functions | SDK supplies the loop (**harness only**); you host | Only tools you define | A custom-tool agent without hand-writing the loop (most cases). Per-turn hooks still give you approval gates, error interception, result modification (e.g. `cache_control`), retries, streaming, and compaction |
| 3 | **Managed Agents** (REST, beta) | Agent config + your tool results | Anthropic supplies the harness **and** hosts a per-session sandbox (**harness + deployment**) | Anthropic-hosted sandbox (bash, files, code exec) + Skills/MCP + your tools | You want Anthropic to run the loop *and* host the per-session workspace; persisted/versioned configs; long-running sessions |
| 4 | **Claude Agent SDK** - *separate product* (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) | A prompt + options | SDK supplies the Claude Code harness + built-in tools (**harness only**); you host | Built-in Read/Write/Edit/Bash/Glob/Grep/WebSearch/WebFetch + MCP + subagents | You want a batteries-included coding/filesystem agent running on your own infra |

The harness/deployment split is the key mental model: options 1, 2, and 4 all **leave deployment to you**; only option 3 (CMA) adds managed deployment. Options 1-3 are what this skill generates; option 4 is a different library with its own docs - see the disambiguation below.

> **Tool Runner != Claude Agent SDK.** These sound alike but are different packages:
> - **Tool Runner** is part of the regular Anthropic API SDK (`anthropic` / `@anthropic-ai/sdk`), reached via `client.beta.messages.tool_runner`. It automates the request -> execute -> loop cycle *for tools you define*. No built-in tools, no filesystem access, no sandbox - you supply every tool and host the compute. It is option 2 above, a thin helper over `POST /v1/messages`.
> - **Claude Agent SDK** (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) is Claude Code packaged as a library. It ships built-in tools (file read/write/edit, bash, grep, web search), the full agent loop, context management, hooks, subagents, permissions, and sessions. You call `query(prompt, options)` and it drives everything.
>
> Both are **harness-only - you host and deploy them.** The difference is scope of harness: the Tool Runner loops over tools *you* define (with per-turn hooks for approval, interception, result modification, and retries - but no built-in tools); the Agent SDK is the full Claude Code harness with built-in tools. Neither provides managed deployment - that's what **Managed Agents (CMA)** adds (Anthropic hosts the loop and a per-session sandbox).
>
> **This skill covers the Claude API and Managed Agents (options 1-3); it does not generate Claude Agent SDK code.** If the user actually wants the Claude Agent SDK, point them to its docs (`code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk`) - don't substitute the API Tool Runner for it, or vice-versa.

### Should I Build an Agent?

Before choosing the agent tier, check all four criteria:

- **Complexity** - Is the task multi-step and hard to fully specify in advance? (e.g., "turn this design doc into a PR" vs. "extract the title from this PDF")
- **Value** - Does the outcome justify higher cost and latency?
- **Viability** - Is Claude capable at this task type?
- **Cost of error** - Can errors be caught and recovered from? (tests, review, rollback)

If the answer is "no" to any of these, stay at a simpler tier (single call or workflow).

---

## Architecture

Everything goes through `POST /v1/messages`. Tools and output constraints are features of this single endpoint - not separate APIs.

**User-defined tools** - You define tools (via decorators, Zod schemas, or raw JSON), and the SDK's tool runner handles calling the API, executing your functions, and looping until Claude is done. For full control, you can write the loop manually.

**Server-side tools** - Anthropic-hosted tools that run on Anthropic's infrastructure. Code execution is fully server-side (declare it in `tools`, Claude runs code automatically). Computer use can be server-hosted or self-hosted.

**Structured outputs** - Constrains the Messages API response format (`output_config.format`) and/or tool parameter validation (`strict: true`). The recommended approach is `client.messages.parse()` which validates responses against your schema automatically. Note: the old `output_format` parameter is deprecated; use `output_config: {format: {...}}` on `messages.create()`.

**Supporting endpoints** - Batches (`POST /v1/messages/batches`), Files (`POST /v1/files`), Token Counting (`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` - see `shared/token-counting.md`), and Models (`GET /v1/models`, `GET /v1/models/{id}` - live capability/context-window discovery) feed into or support Messages API requests.
